content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus identifies the storm/tempest primarily along two complementary lines: (1) divine judgment/wrath and theophany — God's overwhelming power breaking in against the wicked or manifesting his presence (Nahum 1:3; Job 38:1; Jeremiah 23:19; Isaiah 29:6); and (2) in devotional/pastoral usage, the trials and tribulations of the believer's life which Christ calms (Mark 4:35-41; Psalm 107). Secondary alternatives include primordial chaos/chaoskampf, eschatological upheaval of nations (Response A, 'common'), whirlwind as divine transport, and demonic opposition.","book_summary":"The book identifies the storm/tempest as the nations in turmoil — the raging sea of political/national tumult — which Christ stills with 'Peace, be still.' It explicitly flags the common teaching (divine judgment and the trials of life which Christ calms) as the view it departs from, grounding its reading in the sea-noise = tumult-of-people equation (Ps 65:7; Isa 17:12-13; Luke 21:25) and reading Mark 4:39 through that lens.","consensus_core_identification":"Storm = God's judging/theophanic power and, devotionally, the personal trials of life that Christ calms.","book_core_identification":"Storm/raging sea = the nations in turmoil (collective political tumult), rebuked and stilled by Christ.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book reclassifies the flagship consensus case, Mark 4:39, from 'personal trials of life' (and from displays of divine power over nature/chaos) to a typological picture of Christ stilling the raging nations. It retains storm passages tied to national upheaval (Isa 17:12-13; Luke 21:25) — cases the consensus treats as a secondary eschatological alternative — and elevates them to the controlling identification, while excluding the dominant 'storms of life' devotional referent.","material_contradiction":"The consensus's primary referents are divine wrath against the wicked and the individual believer's afflictions; the book denies these are the symbol's meaning ('commonly taught' note) and substitutes a corporate-political referent: the tumultuous nations themselves. The same storm in the same passage (Mark 4) cannot simultaneously be primarily the believer's personal trials and primarily the raging Gentile nations; accepting the book requires replacing the consensus identification, not merely tightening it.","rationale":"Although Response A lists 'eschatological upheaval / political and military turmoil of nations' as a common alternative, no response makes it the core identification, and all four center on judgment/theophany and/or trials of life. The book expressly contrasts itself with that common teaching and installs a different central referent (nations in tumult), reclassifying the key Gospel proof text. Because the central identification is replaced rather than bounded, and Mark 4:39 is materially reassigned, this is DIVERGENT with partial reclassification rather than REFINED; it is not NOVEL because the nations-as-raging-sea motif appears among consensus alternatives.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"The book's reading is essentially the consensus's already-listed 'eschatological upheaval of nations' alternative promoted to primary status, so one could argue the general category (chaotic tumult subdued by God) is preserved and the verdict should be REFINED rather than DIVERGENT. Additionally, the printed citations chiefly concern the sea/waters rather than 'storm, tempest' proper, so the equation may belong more to the Sea & Waters entry than to storm imagery generally.","confidence":"medium"}
